title: How many times?
summary: The quantifiers * + ? {n} {n,m} {n,}, what exactly they repeat, and the empty match that * can find anywhere.

steps.title: Say how many
body: In module 1 you wrote `[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]` for six digits. A **quantifier** says how many times the item
before it repeats, so that becomes `[0-9]{6}`.
| `*` | zero or more | `[0-9]*` also matches nothing |
| `+` | one or more | `[0-9]+` is a whole number |
| `?` | zero or one (optional) | `colou?r` is both spellings |
| `{3}` | exactly three | `[A-Z]{3}` is a currency code |
Below, `[0-9]+ms` finds every duration. Try `[0-9]*ms` and look at the last line: `*` is happy with zero digits.

steps.prompt: Match each quantifier to how many times it repeats the item before it.
steps.explain: `*` is `{0,}`, `+` is `{1,}` and `?` is `{0,1}`. The short forms exist because those three are needed constantly.

steps.title: Order ids, the short way
prompt: Order ids are `ORD-` followed by exactly six ASCII digits: `ORD-004211`. You wrote this in the last boss with six
classes. Write it again with a quantifier. Match the whole string when it is a valid id.

forbid.message: Uses a quantifier instead of repeating the class

hints: One ASCII digit is `[0-9]`. How do you say "exactly six of those"?
steps.explain: `{6}` repeats `[0-9]` exactly six times. Shorter, and nobody has to count the brackets in review.

steps.prompt: Which strings does `ab+` match the **whole** of? Select all that apply.
steps.explain: A quantifier repeats only the **one item** right before it. In `ab+` that is the `b`: one `a`, then one or more `b`. To repeat `ab` as a unit, put it in a group: `(ab)+` (groups are module 4).

steps.title: One item, and the empty match
body: Two rules explain most quantifier surprises.
**A quantifier repeats one item**: a character, a class like `[0-9]`, an escape like `\.`, or a group in brackets.
`https?` makes only the `s` optional. `v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+` repeats each class, not the dot.
**`*` and `?` can match nothing at all.** `[0-9]*` succeeds at every position, so `Regex.Matches` returns empty
matches between the real ones. Below, `a1b22` gives five matches, three of them empty. When you mean "at least
One .NET detail: there are no spaces inside braces. `a{2, 4}` is not a quantifier, it matches the literal text

steps.explain: `[0-9]+` finds `1` and `22`. `[0-9]*` also finds an empty match before `a`, before `b` and at the very end: five in all. `u?` lets the `u` be missing.

steps.title: A version number
prompt: Release tooling reads versions like `1.4.12` and `10.0.100`: three whole numbers separated by dots. Match the whole
string when it is such a version. `1.4`, `1..4` and `1.4.x` are not.
hints: Each number is one or more digits: `[0-9]+`. The dots must be escaped.
steps.explain: Each `+` repeats only its class. With `*` instead, `1..4` would slip through as a version with an empty middle number.

steps.prompt: Complete the two patterns from a deploy script's input checks.
code: // a git commit hash: 7 to 40 lowercase hex characters
steps.explain: The range is written `{min,max}` with a comma and no spaces. `{5,1}` is an error: the minimum cannot exceed the maximum. (`\A` and `\z` pin the pattern to the whole text: module 3.)

steps.title: Big numbers only
prompt: In a billing export, ids under 1000 are test accounts. Find every number with **four or more** digits, and only
In `ids 12, 4521, 99812 and 7` the matches must be exactly `4521` and `99812`.
hints: "At least four" is `{4,}`, with nothing after the comma.
steps.explain: `{4,}` has no upper limit. Each match takes the whole run of digits, so `99812` is one match, not `9981` and `2`.

steps.title: Pull out every number
prompt: Write `List<int> Numbers(string text)` that returns every whole number in `text`, as `int`s, left to right.
A number is a run of one or more ASCII digits. Use `Regex.Matches`, then `int.Parse` each match's `Value`.
template: Dojo.Eq("Numbers(\"retry 3 of 5 after 250ms\")", new List<int> { 3, 5, 250 }, Numbers("retry 3 of 5 after 250ms"));
Dojo.Eq("leading zeros: Numbers(\"007\")", new List<int> { 7 }, Numbers("007"));
Dojo.Eq("no digits gives an empty list", new List<int>(), Numbers("no digits"));
Dojo.Eq("Arabic-Indic digits are not numbers here", new List<int> { 42 }, Numbers("٤٢ and 42"));
hints: `foreach (Match m in Regex.Matches(text, @"[0-9]+"))` visits each number.
Inside the loop: `result.Add(int.Parse(m.Value));`. With `*` instead of `+`, `int.Parse("")` throws.
